statements.justification: Peak values are right, but the claimed SALL1→SALL4→SOX2→NANOG 'wave' is not in the data: NANOG peaks first (9mo), SALL1 and a SOX2 dip at 6mo, SALL4 last (3mo). Shifts of ±0.05 in barely-expressed genes cannot exclude an array artifact; the cited paper shows culture, not fresh blood, raises these genes.

ACOT4 and fatty-acid values are quoted correctly, but the logic is inverted: less thioesterase activity means less free fatty acid released, not more. Fatty acids also rise only at 6–3mo and are lower at 12mo (oleate −0.30) and at SC, while ACOT4 is down throughout, so the two do not track.

ACOT2 values are right, but a +0.04 bump at 9mo does not track the fatty acids, which peak at 6mo when ACOT2 is at baseline. 'The only ACOT' with a bump is false (ACOT9, ACOT6 also rise at 9mo). It explains the same fatty-acid rise as S2 by the opposite mechanism, using mouse data.

Values are right, but the point is empty: a KEGG Alcoholism histone hub is tied to nothing in this cohort and HDAC11/HDAC8 are not relevant. Skin-ageing HDAC data [6] do not transfer to children's blood. Calling 12mo a 'baseline' misreads the design; it is the paper's most informative window.

+0.17 at 12mo, ~0 later, not relevant: correct. HDAC11 does suppress IL-10 in antigen-presenting cells [7]. The hedged prediction fits the paper's IL10 down in cases (IL10 is negative in all five windows here), though the HDAC11 signal is one window in a gene the model did not select.
statements.in_paper_where: Results, 'TNFα activation by ROS accumulation...' (IL10 and TGFβ down, Fig. 6); HDAC11 itself is not mentioned

statements.justification: HDAC8 values and the RIG-I citation are right. Whether weaker interferon signalling follows cannot be settled: interferon genes in the files are mixed (ISG15, IFIT1, MX1 up at 9mo and SC, down or flat at 12 and 3mo), HDAC8 mRNA is only −9% and not relevant, and the evidence is HEK293 overexpression.

APOC3 values are right (−0.005 at 12mo, +0.05 at 3mo, +0.02 at SC). Serum APOC3 does track insulin resistance and coronary calcium in type 1 diabetes [9], but in adults, so 'a lipid shift before autoimmunity' is a loose, properly hedged hypothesis that fits the paper's lipid-impairment theme. The effect is small.
statements.in_paper_where: Abstract; Results 'Lipid metabolism irregularities are linked to decreased nutrient absorption...' (lipid impairment in general); APOC3 itself is not mentioned

statements.justification: All values match, including the largest, LCAT −0.15 at 9mo. Persistent APOA1 down and low phosphatidylcholine are in the paper; adding LCAT, which APOA1 activates, is a coherent hedged hypothesis of impaired HDL maturation, testable by plasma LCAT activity. Weakness: LCAT is liver-made, so blood mRNA is an indirect readout.
statements.in_paper_where: Results 'Lipid metabolism irregularities are linked to decreased nutrient absorption...', Figs 3b and 5 (APOA1 down, phosphatidylcholines down); LCAT is not mentioned

statements.justification: BTD flat to 3mo and +0.14 at SC, HLCS flat or negative: correct. The biotin citations are sound and the text admits the inflammatory direction is unknown. The late timing fits the paper's immune activation at 0–3mo, but no biotin measurement supports a 'biotin-cycle adjustment', and one window has no per-window test.

Values and the lysine pattern are right. The 'late sustained' label is selective, since 12mo (+0.09) is as high as 3mo (+0.10), so the profile zigzags. LysRS having non-canonical immune roles is true but would fit any aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase; hedged as unproven, so acceptable but weak.

Values match: C1QB −0.07 to +0.11, C1QC −0.01 to +0.06. But none of C1QA/B/C is relevant, and all three are positive at SC, so splitting them into 'rising' and 'baseline shift' reads noise. A late C1q rise fits the paper's 0–3mo immune activation, hedged as undetermined; complement is not in the paper.

Values match (GALR3 +0.01 to +0.04 in all windows; GAL −0.06 at 6mo). The mouse psoriasis knockout supports a pro-inflammatory GALR3, but the rat thymocyte paper shows an antiproliferative effect, and a 'tonic' tone is untestable from mRNA shifts this small. Weak and speculative; acceptable only because it is hedged.

CARD6 +0.11/+0.16 at 12/9mo and non-relevant RIPK2 are right; the cited work shows CARD6 binds RIPK2/NOD1 and blocks their NF-κB induction. 'Modulation' is cautious, but a CARD6 rise would damp NF-κB, opposite to the paper's inflammation theme; the data cannot say if protein function changes.

The −0.08 dip is the APC2 row, a different gene (Wnt pathway), not APOC2. The real APOC2 row is not relevant and peaks +0.10 at 9mo. The CREB3L3 peak is also at 6mo, the same time, not 'opposite'. Less TG clearance also contradicts the lower triglyceride class in cases at every window.

overall.comment: Numbers are mostly quoted accurately and several statements (APOA1/phosphatidylcholine/LCAT, HDAC11 with IL10) connect sensibly to the paper's lipid-impairment and IL10-down findings, but most statements hang literature on single, tiny (about ±0.05 log2), often non-relevant genes. It never reaches the paper's main conclusions (glycolysis/OXPHOS/ROS, arachidonate, TNF, MMP9/TIMP3, cytotoxicity), and it contains real errors: APC2 read as APOC2, an inverted ACOT4 mechanism, a misread SALL/NANOG 'wave', and 12mo treated as a 'baseline'.
